aiExplanation: This is a **brute-force approach** that finds the minimum cost by trying all possible combinations of three elements where the first element is always `nums[0]`, and the other two elements are chosen from the remaining positions. The nested loops iterate through all valid pairs `(i, j)` where `1 <= i < j < n`, calculate `nums[0] + nums[i] + nums[j]` for each combination, and keep track of the minimum value encountered. While this guarantees finding the correct answer, it has **O(n²) time complexity** since it examines every possible pair.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This **optimized solution** recognizes that to minimize the total cost, you need the first element `nums[0]` plus the two smallest elements from the rest of the array. It creates a copy of all elements except the first one, sorts this copy in ascending order, and then simply returns `nums[0]` plus the first two elements of the sorted array (which are the two smallest). This approach has **O(n log n) time complexity** due to sorting, which is much more efficient than trying all combinations, and the code is also cleaner and easier to understand.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is the **most efficient solution** that finds the two minimum values in a single pass through the array without any sorting. It maintains two variables `min1` (smallest value) and `min2` (second smallest value), iterating through the array once and updating them as it encounters smaller values. When a new element is smaller than or equal to `min1`, it shifts `min1` to `min2` and updates `min1`; otherwise, if it's smaller than `min2`, just update `min2`. Finally, it returns `nums[0]` plus these two minimums. With **O(n) time complexity** and **O(1) space complexity**, this is both faster and more memory-efficient than the sorting approach.
